newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Afghan turmoil sends shockwaves through C. Asia.
newsitem.headline: Afghan turmoil sends shockwaves through C. Asia.

text.p: The turmoil in Afghanistan after the Islamist Taleban militia seized the capital Kabul last week has sent shockwaves through its neighbours, the former Soviet republics in Central Asia to the north.
Leaders in the five Central Asian states fear any brand of radical Islam and the unrest it could spark in their own ethnically diverse nations.

They also fear that Russia, their former colonial master, could use any spread in radical Islam to the ex-Soviet republics to strengthen its influence over the young states and their vast energy and mineral resources.
Afghanistan borders three of Central Asia's five states -- Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.
They had complained even before the Taleban militia victory of Afghanistan's potentially destabilising influence.
Afghanistan's most obvious influence is in Tajikistan, where a four-year civil war between the government and Islamic fighters has killed tens of thousands and displaced more.

Afghan warlord Ahmad Shah Masood, himself an ethnic Tajik, and other Afghan factions have allowed the guerrillas to set up bases and train in the mountains across the Amu Darya river which separates the two mountainous countries.
The Tajik Islamic leader Sayed Abdullo Nuri is based in the northern Afghan town of Taloqan, while thousands of refugees from Tajikistan shelter in dust-blown camps inside Afghanistan.
A sizeable part of the Afghan drug trade is now routed through Central Asia, bringing its own problems of crime, corruption and addiction.
The Taleban's radical brand of Islam is even less welcome to Central Asian governments.
Human rights organisations say Islamic leaders have been imprisoned in Uzbekistan, which fears Islam as a grass roots base for political opposition.

Uzbekistan's state-controlled television, monitored by the British Broadcasting Corporation, expressed "serious concern and alarm" at the crisis in Afghanistan after a special session of the country's National Security Council on Tuesday.
But Uzbek President Islam Karimov, due in the Kazakh capital Almaty on Friday to attend a special Commonwealth of Independent States summit on Afghanistan, has kept his own counsel.
Diplomats say Uzbekistan has provided low-key support like representative offices in the republic to a powerful faction which stands in the way of complete Taleban control of Afghanistan.
The Jumbish-i-Milli faction of ethnic Uzbek warlord, General Abdul Rashid Dostum, holds northern territory next to Uzbekistan.

"The Uzbeks are probably pressuring Dostum to do a deal with the Taleban," said a Western diplomat recently based in the region. He said any talk of a Taleban invasion of Central Asia was "pie in the sky".
But most Afghans in territory controlled by Dostum believe it will not be long before the Taleban try and take the north.
This would give Russia an excuse to try and beef up its presence in the region, citing instability along vulnerable southern borders.
The diplomat said Russian security supremo Alexander Lebed's call for aid for factions opposed to the Taleban reflected Russia's deep desire to rebuild its influence in Central Asia.
Thousands of Russian troops already prop up the weak Tajik government.

"The Russians are pushing Uzbekistan to support Dostum, which would inevitably involve Russia," the diplomat said. "This is the last thing Uzbekistan wants which is to build itself as an independent state."

The image of tearaway gunmen does little for Afghanistan's investment image, but it plays an important part in the tangled fight for influence over trade and oil export routes from land-locked Central Asia to Western and other Asian markets.
Russia, which now controls all the existing pipeline routes out of Central Asia, is fighting hard to hold onto its monopoly.
